title: Divergence
body:
How much a [[Vector Field]] is spreading out at a point. Input a vector field, output a **scalar**.

$$
\operatorname{div}\mathbf{F} = \nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} = \frac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial R}{\partial z}
$$

for $\mathbf{F} = \langle P, Q, R\rangle$. The notation is literal: treat
$\nabla = \langle \partial_x, \partial_y, \partial_z \rangle$ as a vector of operators and take the
[[Dot Product]]. A dot product returns a number, which is the shape check.

## What the sign means

Put a tiny closed box around the point and ask whether more fluid leaves than enters.

| Sign | Reading |
|---|---|
| $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} > 0$ | **source**: net outflow, the field is spreading |
| $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} < 0$ | **sink**: net inflow, the field is converging |
| $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} = 0$ | **incompressible** (solenoidal): whatever flows in flows out |

That is not a metaphor. The [[Divergence Theorem]] makes it exact: divergence is **[[Flux]] per
unit volume**, in the limit as the volume shrinks to the point.

```
F = ⟨x, y⟩          div F = 1 + 1 = 2      everything flows outward, uniform source
F = ⟨-y, x⟩         div F = 0 + 0 = 0      pure rotation, nothing spreads
F = ⟨-x, -y⟩        div F = -2             everything flows inward, a sink
```

The middle example is the one to remember: **rotation contributes nothing to divergence**. The two
operators measure genuinely independent things, which is why a field needs both [[Curl]] and
divergence to be pinned down.
